summary:
Sort, then for each **different** first value `a[i]`, squeeze `j`, `k` over the rest looking for
`a[j] + a[k] = −a[i]`. After a hit, move `j` past copies of `a[j]` so the same triple isn't found again; skip
repeated first values too. Triples come out already sorted. O(n²).

question.md:
Find every **different** triple of values (from three different positions) summing to 0. Each triple is written
in increasing order, and the list is sorted.

- **Duplicates in the input** must not create duplicate triples: `[-1, 0, 1]` is reported once.
- **Up to 2000 values.**

think.md:
`[-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4, 2, -2]` gives `[[-4, 2, 2], [-2, 0, 2], [-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]`.

The 3-sum squeeze finds every triple, but with repeated values it would find some more than once. Two skips fix
that, both easy because equal values sit together after sorting: skip a first value equal to the previous
first value, and after recording a triple, step `j` past every copy of the value just used.

approaches.title: Every triple, deduplicated with a set

idea.md: Check every triple; store each zero-sum triple, sorted, in a set; return the set sorted.

notes.c: No set in C: collect all triples, then sort and drop repeats.

lines.text: Store the triple in increasing order, so equal triples look identical.

notes.c: Sort, then keep only the first copy of each triple; each row has 3 columns.

complexity.md: **Time O(n³).** **Space O(t)** for the t triples found.

limits.md: About 1.3 × 10⁹ triples at n = 2000, plus a set to remove repeats. Sorting first lets the squeeze find each distinct triple once and skip duplicates by comparing neighbours.

approaches.title: Sort, fix one, squeeze, skip duplicates

idea.md: Sort. For each `i` (skipping `a[i] == a[i−1]`; stopping once `a[i] > 0`), squeeze `j`, `k`: sum < 0 → `j++`, > 0 → `k−−`, = 0 → record, then advance `j` past equal values and decrease `k`.

build: Squeeze; on a hit, skip repeated second values.

lines.text: Sort a copy; triples will come out in increasing order automatically.
A first value equal to the previous one would find exactly the same triples: skip it.
If the smallest of the three is positive, no sum can be 0 from here on.
Record the triple, then move `j` past every copy of this second value (the third value is then forced, so `k` moves too).

notes.c: The output array grows by doubling; each row has 3 columns.

complexity.md: **Time O(n²).** **Space O(1)** besides the sorted copy and the output.

steps.text: -1 is the same first value as before: skip it (it would find the same triples).

walk.title: Sort. Fix each different first value, squeeze for pairs summing to its negative, and skip repeated values so no triple is reported twice.

takeaways.md:
- **Distinct 3-sum:** sort, skip equal first values, and after each hit skip equal second values.
- Sorting makes duplicates adjacent, so a neighbour comparison replaces a hash set.
- Early exit: once the fixed value is positive, a zero sum is impossible.
